author: assistant sub-agent V3G1-TR54 (v3 re-map); fix pass Fix1

vectors.enisa_quote: transmitting erroneous data for malicious purposes via what appears to be a legitimate signal
vectors.reason: The adversary transmits a signal that looks legitimate, from outside the mission, over the radio link.

vectors.enisa_quote: launched on sensor data and/or guidance control
vectors.reason: The text names sensor data but not who attacks or from where; optical or electrical stimulation of sensors (EX-0014.03: 'injected electrically at interfaces, optically (blinding/dazzling trackers or sun sensors)') can only be done from close range, so proximity is the best-supported origin.

rows.reason: Overwhelming the telemetry downlink so it never arrives is jamming (TR44 keeps it), whereas this ENISA text is about a signal that looks legitimate, not one drowned out.
Muting telemetry publishers or packet filters on board is an inside manipulation of the spacecraft; ENISA describes a forged signal arriving from outside, with no on-board suppression.
Zeroing or freezing the Vehicle Command Counter hides accepted commands; ENISA speaks of deceiving the receiver with a legitimate-looking signal, not of covering counters afterwards.
Clearing or forging the rejected-command counter hides trial-and-error probing, which the ENISA spoofing text never mentions.
Tampering with command-receiver gain (AGC) stops commands from being processed, which is telecommand suppression (TR32), not the forged signal described here.
Using or masking receiver lock indicators (bit/frame/command lock) to validate geometry or hide readiness is not what a spoofed signal that looks legitimate does.
Switching on-orbit crypto modes or 'crypto off' states to desynchronise ground and spacecraft is a separate protection-bypass step that ENISA does not mention.

Spoofing GPS ephemeris so the satellite mis-estimates its position is already carried by EX-0014.04 (false position/velocity/time); this row is its Defense-Evasion variant that conceals activity, which ENISA does not describe.
Dazzling or fooling the spacecraft's proximity-awareness sensors hides an approaching vehicle from SSA; ENISA describes deceiving the receiver with data, not hiding an approach.
Replay as a general technique also covers crosslinks and internal buses; only its telecommand-packet child fits the 'malicious commands' wording, so the parent adds no step of its own.
Retransmitting messages on the internal bus (1553, SpaceWire) needs a foothold already on board; ENISA's spoofer transmits from outside via a signal that appears legitimate.
Toggling flags or algorithms to process traffic in clear or with weak protection is the SLE/SDL protocol compromise of TR28; ENISA spoofing text does not describe defeating the protection.
Inducing single-event upsets by charge or radiation effects is a hardware-fault attack; the ENISA spoofing text names only forged data and signals.
Saturating the spacecraft with valid commands to burn resources is flooding (TR40), not forging a legitimate-looking signal.
Injecting noise or malformed frames so receivers labour to reject them is not a signal that appears legitimate; the ENISA spoofing text speaks of believable data.
Forging or biasing the time seen by onboard consumers is not named by ENISA, and false time delivered by a spoofed navigation signal is already covered by EX-0014.04 (false position/velocity/time).
Forging frames on the internal bus (1553, SpaceWire, CAN) is done from inside the spacecraft; ENISA's spoofing arrives as a signal at the receiver or sensor.
Jamming denies a signal with RF energy, whereas the ENISA text describes a believable signal, not denial of one.
Driving uplink Eb/N0 below the demodulator threshold blocks telecommands (jamming, TR44), the opposite of a forged but legitimate-looking uplink.
Downlink jammers create noise at the ground receiver; ENISA's erroneous data to the ground stations is data content, not noise on the carrier.
Raising the noise floor in GNSS bands so signals are not tracked denies navigation; ENISA spoofing is about false navigation data, which EX-0014.04 covers, not its denial.
Physically striking space assets is the kinetic attack of TR18; spoofing text is about forged data.
A direct-ascent missile that destroys a satellite in orbit is the ASAT threat (TR18), unrelated to deceiving a receiver.
A co-orbital vehicle that collides or detonates near the target is the ASAT threat (TR18), not signal spoofing.
Re-sending valid commands to make the spacecraft dump data again, then capturing the downlink, is data theft; ENISA states no theft.
Timing acknowledgments and framing gaps to learn which code ran is a side-channel leak that the spoofing text does not describe.
Capturing mission traffic in transit is interception (TR29); the spoofer here transmits rather than listens.
Collecting telecommand frames from the uplink is interception (TR29) and gives the adversary nothing that ENISA's forged signal requires as a described step.
Recording telemetry and playbacks off the downlink is interception (TR29), not erroneous data sent to a receiver.
Co-opting a secondary link (rekeying, beacon, crosslink) as a covert data path is exfiltration; ENISA's spoofing sends data in, not out.
A nearby vehicle collecting emissions as a mobile TEMPEST sensor is listening, while spoofing is transmitting forged data.
Retuning or reconfiguring the radio so mission data leaves over unmonitored paths is exfiltration, which ENISA's spoofing text does not state.
Remapping transponder input-output paths toward non-mission receivers is exfiltration through a transponder, not forged data to the receiver.
Implanting code in a payload or its gateway to route data out is a payload compromise (TR46), not spoofing.
Inserting malicious code or hardware during manufacturing and delivery is the supply-chain origin; ENISA's spoofer acts on a live signal, not before flight.
Poisoned dependencies, base images or build tools are a pre-flight software-supply-chain door; the ENISA spoofing text has no development-stage actor.
Swapping signed binaries or update metadata upstream of the build is software-supply-chain compromise (TR55), unlike a spoofed in-flight signal.
Hardware Trojans in ASIC/FPGA designs before delivery are a supply-chain door, and the ENISA text names no such actor.
Compromising an SDR's waveform, bitstream or flowgraph gives a programmable foothold inside the radio; ENISA's spoofer stays outside and only imitates a legitimate signal.
Using a compromised neighbour's crosslink trust as a bridgehead is a space-segment lateral door, with no crosslink actor in the ENISA spoofing text.
Reaching the spacecraft through a backup or contingency communication path differing from the primary TT&C is not described; ENISA names only a signal that looks legitimate.
Establishing presence on a standby MOC or alternate ground station is a ground compromise that ENISA's spoofing text does not describe.
Targeting the secondary receive path (alternate antenna or cross-strapped front end) is a variant door; ENISA does not distinguish primary from backup receivers.
Manoeuvring to approach the target for local sensing or signalling is rendezvous and proximity; ENISA gives no approach and the proximity vector enters through counterspace IA-0008.03.
Analysing unintentional emissions from crypto modules and decoders is listening, not transmission of forged data.
Exploiting a docking or OSAM bridge between vehicles needs a servicing event the ENISA spoofing text never mentions.
Grappling the target with a robotic arm or coupler is physical contact; ENISA's sensor spoofing needs no capture.
Entering through a hosted payload's command set and telemetry path is a hosted-payload door; ENISA names no hosted payload.
Compromising operator workstations and mission-control software is a ground-system takeover; ENISA's attacker transmits a signal rather than owning ground systems.
Tampering with the software-update pipeline of an on-orbit vehicle is the update compromise of TR46, not spoofing.
Sending legitimate-looking commands from a compromised mission-owned ground system needs control of the ground; ENISA's spoofer fakes a signal from outside.
A rogue spacecraft that phases into a local-peer orbit and radiates narrow-band signals is an RF-geometry foothold; ENISA gives no space-based transmitter.
Riding connections the mission already trusts (partners, vendors) is third-party compromise, with no trust relationship in the ENISA spoofing text.
Compromising university or international collaborators' portals and credentials is not described by ENISA.
Abusing a vendor's remote administration and licence routes into operations is not described by ENISA.
Compromising SATCOM terminals or customer gateways in the user segment is not described; ENISA's receiver and ground-station ends are not user equipment.
Timing the first execution to safe-mode, when the vehicle relaxes controls, is an opportunity choice that ENISA does not state.
Infecting removable media or auxiliary interfaces during I&T or on orbit is a physical-access door absent from the spoofing text.
Compromising test controllers, EGSE and loaders during assembly, test and launch is a pre-launch door that ENISA does not name.
Pivoting from the host spacecraft into a hosted payload is a bus-to-payload door not mentioned in the ENISA text.
Triggering functions that already exist for harmful use is not what ENISA says; its spoofing yields forged data and commands, with no abuse of a native function.
Forcing or holding a mode or mission-phase change is not stated by ENISA; the 'guidance control' phrase names a target of spoofing, not a mode transition.
Rewriting thresholds, gains and access rules in non-executable settings is configuration tampering (TR57), not forged input.
Replacing code, firmware or logic is software manipulation (TR42); spoofing alters the input the code sees, not the code.
Depleting or monopolising a finite resource is exhaustion (TR51), not data forged to look legitimate.
Shifting the on-board clock or breaking synchronisation is a timing effect; ENISA names no timing consequence, only malicious commands and erroneous data.
Pivoting through the host-payload gateway is lateral movement after access; ENISA's spoofing has no on-board movement.
Hopping to other satellites over crosslinks is lateral movement across the constellation, with no crosslink in the ENISA text.
Replacing keys to lock out operators is takeover persistence (TR52), unlike spoofing that merely forges input.
Stealing keys or PN codes that confer command authority prepares authenticated access; ENISA's signal only appears legitimate, with no key theft named.
Pre-positioning tooling and C2 pipelines on adversary infrastructure does not enable any kept spoofing row beyond ground equipment already covered.
Staging exploits, malicious tables and patch images prepares an execution foothold, whereas no kept row here uploads a payload.
Studying crypto algorithms, anti-replay windows and counters prepares defeating protections, which no kept row needs.
Scanning payload downlinks, user terminals and crosslinks to find extra RF surfaces is not needed by the TT&C-band spoofing row.
Gathering credentials and TT&C keys is preparation for authenticated access; the ENISA spoofer only imitates a legitimate signal.
Capturing mission communications broadly is generic eavesdropping; only its uplink-intercept child supports a kept row.
Active probing to elicit frequencies and device behaviour is scanning that no kept spoofing row depends on.
Acquiring or assembling an own RF ground stack is the equipment the rogue ground station needs to transmit the forged signal.
Frequency, modulation and framing details of the mission link are needed so the spoofed signal passes as legitimate.
Knowing the telecommand protocol, framing and authentication fields is what lets forged commands reach the satellite.
Capturing uplink traffic supplies the accepted telecommands that a replay resends.

DE-0002 conceals an intruder from operators by manipulating telemetry or disabling telemetry software, while ENISA's erroneous data to the ground stations is a spoofing outcome and no RF-origin technique here delivers false telemetry to a ground receiver.

rows.enisa_quote: what appears to be a legitimate signal
rows.sparta_quote: The adversary presents themselves as an authorized origin so activity appears legitimate across RF, protocol, and organizational boundaries
rows.reason: Presenting as an authorised origin is what makes the forged signal look legitimate to the receiver.

rows.enisa_quote: malicious comands being sent to the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: resend authentic-looking telecommands that were previously accepted by the spacecraft
rows.reason: ENISA does not name replay; a resent captured telecommand is a signal that appears legitimate and carries a malicious command, which is how the text's 'malicious comands being sent' can be realised (inference).

rows.sparta_quote: The adversary forges inputs that subsystems treat as trustworthy truth
rows.reason: Forged inputs that the receiver treats as genuine are the spoofing ENISA describes.
rows.link_only_reason: Forged time tags, bus messages or telecommand-borne data are accepted only after the spacecraft takes the frame past link authentication; the RF-layer navigation spoof is carried by EX-0014.04, which needs only the GNSS link.

rows.enisa_quote: launched on sensor data and/or guidance control
rows.sparta_quote: The attacker presents fabricated or biased measurements that estimation and control treat as ground truth
rows.reason: ENISA names spoofing of sensor data; the SPARTA spoofs are injected electrically or optically at the sensor, so they need close range.

rows.enisa_quote: launched on sensor data and/or guidance control
rows.reason: Guidance control is fed by the navigation solution, so a transmitted false navigation signal is spoofing of guidance input; it also covers false time. The signal reaches the receiver over the GNSS link, not the telecommand uplink.

rows.sparta_quote: Most interact by radiating or exchanging traffic using mission-compatible waveforms, framing, or crosslink protocols
rows.reason: An external transmitter using mission-compatible waveforms is the origin of the spoofed signal.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: A rogue ground station is the transmitter that sends the signal that appears legitimate.

rows.sparta_quote: directed-energy systems can dazzle sensors or upset electronics
rows.reason: A counterspace platform close to the satellite is the actor-controlled node that can dazzle its sensors, the entry for sensor-data spoofing.

rows.link_only_reason: A spoofed navigation signal or sensor stimulus falsifies on-board data without any telecommand being accepted, so SDLS does not remove it.
rows.enisa_quote: transmitting erroneous data for malicious purposes
rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may falsify, suppress, replace, delete, or corrupt this information
rows.reason: Realises the erroneous data that on-board consumers (sensors, navigation solution) accept as genuine.

rows.enisa_quote: malicious comands being sent to the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may inject an unauthorized command or alter a legitimate command before execution
rows.reason: Realises malicious commands reaching the satellite; it needs an accepted command, so SDLS rightly removes it.

review_response.finding: DE-0002 does not do what ENISA says (conceals an intruder; no RF technique delivers false telemetry to ground)
review_response.action: fixed: DE-0002 demoted to D-UNDESCRIBED. Limit: no SPARTA technique delivers false telemetry to the ground station from an RF origin, so 'erroneous data to the ground stations' is not modelled; IMP-0010 is kept for sensor/PNT outcomes only.

review_response.finding: S3: EX-0014.03 sensor spoofing unreachable by an RF transmitter
review_response.action: fixed: EX-0014.03 moved to the new proximity vector (weak basis) with IA-0008.03 as entry (also kept by TR18).

review_response.finding: S1: IMP-0010/IMP-0011 removed under SDLS although the spoof survives
review_response.action: fixed: IMP-0010 is link_only with a reason (spoofed input falsifies data with no telecommand). IMP-0011 kept because command injection needs an accepted command: SDLS-on assumes an intact protocol, so removal is right; EX-0006/EX-0003 are not link_only here.

review_response.finding: EX-0001.01 replay is an inference, not ENISA-stated
review_response.action: kept because it is a plausible means for 'malicious commands'; the row reason now says it is a judgement from 'what appears to be a legitimate signal'.

review_response.finding: S4: EX-0014 plus EX-0014.03/.04 parent/child pattern; EX-0014.01 vs PNT time; IMP-0014
review_response.action: kept because the quotes differ: parent covers RF spoof of the receiver, .03 sensors (proximity), .04 PNT (rf_link); the engine treats each by its link_only list. EX-0014.01 stays D-UNDESCRIBED since EX-0014.04 covers false position/velocity/time; IMP-0014 stays D-UNDESCRIBED as ENISA names no timing effect.

review_response.finding: Vector limit: spoofing on both the receiver and the transmitter end
review_response.action: kept because the surface model has only the satellite receiver as target; a ground-station target does not exist in the surface model. Stated as a limit.

review_response.finding: No-issue items (rf_link vector, IA-0008/.01 entries, DE-0004, P-PREP rows, D-OTHER to TR44/TR29/TR18)
review_response.action: kept; all reasons rewritten one per row, D-OTHER targets re-checked for reciprocity (EX-0006 now TR28).

review_response.finding: fix pass M3: GNSS spoof reaches the bus over a TT&C uplink path and EX-0014 parent is link-only by default
review_response.action: fixed: the surface now has a GNSS link, so EX-0014.04 needs only that link and its reason says so; EX-0014 gets link_only false with a reason (bus and time-tag forgery needs an accepted frame), so under SDLS only the GNSS-borne spoof and its link-only outcome survive.

review_response.finding: fix pass M5: ground-end spoofing limit and SDLS caveat not in the file
fix pass m10: DE-0004 K-ENABLE here, K-ACTION in TR43/TR37/TR35
review_response.action: kept because the role differs: here masquerade only makes the forged signal look legitimate (it enables EX-0014); in TR43/TR37/TR35 masquerade is the threat itself.

notes: Not covered: ENISA's 'erroneous data to the ground stations' (spoofing toward the receiving ground end) has no technique and no attack-surface target; only the satellite receiver is modelled.
SDLS-on results assume an intact protocol; the GNSS spoof (EX-0014.04, IMP-0010 link_only) survives SDLS because it does not use the telecommand uplink, command spoofing (IMP-0011) does not.
